1 --- 2 title: Designing view transitions 3 description: Learn how to use view transitions to communicate meaning during navigation, loading, and content changes in a Next.js app. 4 nav_title: View transitions 5 --- 6 7 In web apps, route changes replace the entire page at once. One set of elements disappears, another appears, with no visual connection between them. A user selects a photo thumbnail to view it in detail on another page. They are the same image, but nothing on screen communicates that. 8 9 Apps that need these transitions typically rely on complex animation libraries that manage mount/unmount lifecycles, track element positions across routes, and coordinate timing manually, to animate how elements enter, exit, and move between states. 10 11 React's `` component integrates with the browser's [View Transitions API](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/View_Transition_API) to handle this declaratively. You name the elements that should persist, and the browser animates between their old and new positions. 12 13 This guide walks through four patterns that cover the most common cases: morphing shared elements, animating loading states, adding directional navigation, and crossfading content within the same route. 14 15 ## Use the vercel-react-view-transitions skill 16 17 The [`vercel-react-view-transitions`](https://github.com/vercel-labs/agent-skills/tree/main/skills/react-view-transitions) skill teaches a coding agent the patterns in this guide, plus the CSS recipes and troubleshooting for applying them to an existing app. 18 19 Install the skill: 20 21 ```bash filename="Terminal" 22 npx skills add https://github.com/vercel-labs/agent-skills --skill vercel-react-view-transitions 23 ``` 24 25 Then give the agent this prompt: 26 27 ```prompt 28 Add view transitions to this app using the vercel-react-view-transitions skill. 29 ``` 30 31 To apply the patterns yourself, follow the walkthrough below. 32 33 ## Example 34 35 As an example, we'll build a photography gallery called _Frames_. 36 37 We'll start by morphing a thumbnail into a hero image (shared elements), then animate the loading skeleton into real content (Suspense reveals), add directional slides for forward and back navigation (route transitions), and finish with crossfades for switching between photographer tabs (same-route transitions). 38 39 You can find the resources used in this example here: 40 41 - [Demo](https://react-view-transitions-demo.labs.vercel.dev) 42 - [Code](https://github.com/vercel-labs/react-view-transitions-demo) 43 44 View transitions work in the App Router with no configuration. The App Router uses [React canary releases](https://react.dev/blog/2023/05/03/react-canaries), which contain all stable React 19 changes as well as newer features like `ViewTransition`. You do not need to install `react@canary` yourself. 45 46 > [!NOTE] 47 > React's integration uses newer View Transitions API features (transition types and `view-transition-class`), available in Chromium 125+ and recent Safari and Firefox versions. Some animations may behave differently in Safari. Without browser support, your application works normally; the transitions do not animate. 48 49 Import the `ViewTransition` component from React: 50 51 ```tsx 52 import { ViewTransition } from 'react' 53 ``` 54 55 `` animations are activated by [Transitions](https://react.dev/reference/react/useTransition), [``](https://react.dev/reference/react/Suspense), and [`useDeferredValue`](https://react.dev/reference/react/useDeferredValue). Regular `setState` calls do not trigger them. In Next.js, route navigations are transitions, so `` animations activate automatically during navigation. 56 57 ### Step 1: Morph a thumbnail into a hero image 58 59 The gallery displays photos in a grid. Clicking a photo opens a detail page with a larger version of the same image. Without transitions, the thumbnail disappears and the hero appears. Nothing connects them visually. The user has to scan the detail page to confirm they clicked the right photo. 60 61 In motion design, when an object persists across a cut, it communicates continuity. The viewer understands they are looking at the same thing, not a replacement. This is the most important transition pattern: **shared element morphing**. 62 63 Wrap both the grid thumbnail and the detail hero in `` with the same `name`: 64 65 ```tsx filename="components/photo-grid.tsx" 66 import { ViewTransition } from 'react' 67 import Image from 'next/image' 68 import Link from 'next/link' 69 70 function PhotoGrid({ photos }) { 71 return ( 72
73 {photos.map((photo) => ( 74 75 76 77 78 79 ))} 80
81 ) 82 } 83 ``` 84 85 ```tsx filename="app/photo/[id]/photo-content.tsx" 86 import { ViewTransition } from 'react' 87 import Image from 'next/image' 88 89 async function PhotoContent({ id }) { 90 const photo = await getPhoto(id) 91 92 return ( 93 94
95 96
97 98 ) 99 } 100 ``` 101 102 The `name` prop creates identity. React finds elements with the same name on the old and new pages, then animates between their size and position automatically. No additional props are needed for the morph to work. 103 104 If we click a thumbnail now, the image scales and repositions from its grid cell to the hero slot. Navigating back reverses the morph. The user sees one object moving, not two objects swapping. 105 106 The morph plays when the destination content renders in the same commit as the navigation, which is the case with prefetched (cached) pages. If the destination suspends into a fallback first, no pair forms, and the content animates with its enter animation instead when it arrives. 107 108 #### Customizing the morph animation 109 110 The morph works without any CSS. To customize it, add `share="morph"` together with `default="none"`. The `share` prop assigns the `morph` class to the view transition, which you can target with CSS pseudo-elements. For example, to soften the morph mid-flight with a [`blur`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/filter-function/blur) keyframe: 111 112 ```tsx 113 114 115 116 ``` 117 118 Add the same props to both Step 1 snippets (`photo-grid.tsx` and `photo-content.tsx`). `default="none"` keeps each named image from running its own crossfade on every unrelated transition. Without it, every named `` animates whenever any transition runs on the page. When you add `default="none"` to a named pair, keep the explicit `share`. With `default="none"` and no `share` prop, the pair silently stops morphing. 119 120 ```css filename="app/globals.css" 121 ::view-transition-group(.morph) { 122 animation-duration: 400ms; 123 } 124 ::view-transition-image-pair(.morph) { 125 animation-name: via-blur; 126 } 127 @keyframes via-blur { 128 30% { 129 filter: blur(3px); 130 } 131 } 132 ``` 133 134 The blur hides pixel-level interpolation artifacts during the transition. At 400ms, the morph is slow enough to register but fast enough to feel direct. 135 136 ### Step 2: Animate loading states with Suspense reveals 137 138 The photo detail page loads its content asynchronously. While data is in flight, a Suspense boundary shows a skeleton. When the data resolves, the skeleton is replaced by the real content. 139 140 Without a transition, the swap is instant. The skeleton vanishes and the content pops in. 141 142 In motion design, vertical direction encodes hierarchy. Content sliding up communicates arrival. Content sliding down communicates departure. The pair together creates a handoff: the placeholder yields to the real thing. 143 144 Wrap the Suspense fallback in a `ViewTransition` with an exit animation, and the content in a `ViewTransition` with an enter animation: 145 146 ```tsx filename="app/photo/[id]/page.tsx" 147 import { Suspense, ViewTransition } from 'react' 148 149 export default async function PhotoPage({ params }) { 150 const { id } = await params 151 152 return ( 153 156 157 158 } 159 > 160 161 162 163 164 ) 165 } 166 ``` 167 168 As in Step 1, `default="none"` prevents this `ViewTransition` from animating during unrelated transitions, like the shared element morph. 169 170 The CSS animations use asymmetric timing. The exit is fast (150ms). The enter fade is slower (210ms) and delayed until the exit completes, while its slide movement runs longer (400ms): 171 172 ```css filename="app/globals.css" 173 :root { 174 --duration-exit: 150ms; 175 --duration-enter: 210ms; 176 --duration-move: 400ms; 177 } 178 179 ::view-transition-old(.slide-down) { 180 animation: 181 var(--duration-exit) ease-out both fade reverse, 182 var(--duration-exit) ease-out both slide-y reverse; 183 } 184 ::view-transition-new(.slide-up) { 185 animation: 186 var(--duration-enter) ease-in var(--duration-exit) both fade, 187 var(--duration-move) ease-in both slide-y; 188 } 189 190 @keyframes fade { 191 from { 192 filter: blur(3px); 193 opacity: 0; 194 } 195 to { 196 filter: blur(0); 197 opacity: 1; 198 } 199 } 200 @keyframes slide-y { 201 from { 202 transform: translateY(10px); 203 } 204 to { 205 transform: translateY(0); 206 } 207 } 208 ``` 209 210 The asymmetry is deliberate. Old content should leave quickly so it does not compete for attention. New content should arrive more gently so the user has time to register it. The `var(--duration-exit)` delay on the enter fade means the new content waits for the old content to finish leaving before it becomes visible. 211 212 If we refresh the page, the skeleton slides down and fades out, and a moment later the real content slides up and fades in. 213 214 ### Step 3: Add directional motion for navigation 215 216 The gallery now has morphing images and animated loading states. But navigating between pages still has no directional signal. Forward and back navigations look identical. The user cannot tell from the animation whether they moved deeper into the app or returned to a previous page. 217 218 In film and animation, horizontal direction encodes spatial position. Moving left means progressing forward (like turning a page in a left-to-right language). Moving right means going back. This convention is so ingrained that violating it feels disorienting. 219 220 Use the `transitionTypes` prop on `` to tag forward navigations: 221 222 ```tsx filename="components/photo-grid.tsx" 223 224 {/* photo thumbnail */} 225 226 ``` 227 228 The same pattern works for any navigation within the app. For example, previous/next arrows on a photo detail page can use `nav-back` and `nav-forward` to animate in the corresponding direction. 229 230 For links that return the user to a previous page, use `nav-back`: 231 232 ```tsx filename="app/photo/[id]/page.tsx" 233 234 ← Gallery 235 236 ``` 237 238 The transition type is not automatic. You decide which links are "forward" and which are "back" based on your app's navigation hierarchy. 239 240 Then wrap page content in a `ViewTransition` that maps transition types to directional animations: 241 242 ```tsx filename="app/photo/[id]/page.tsx" 243 256 {/* page content */} 257 258 ``` 259 260 The `enter` and `exit` props accept an object keyed by transition type. When a navigation carries the `nav-forward` type, the exit animation slides old content left and the enter animation slides new content in from the right. The `default: "none"` ensures that transitions without a type (browser back/forward, `router.refresh()`, Suspense reveals) produce no directional animation. 261 262 Wrap every participating page the same way. For the gallery to slide out on forward navigation and back in on `nav-back`, its page needs the same wrapper. Put the wrapper in each `page.tsx`, not the layout. Layouts persist across navigations, so enter and exit never fire there: 263 264 ```tsx filename="app/page.tsx" 265 278 279 280 ``` 281 282 The CSS for directional slides: 283 284 ```css filename="app/globals.css" 285 ::view-transition-old(.nav-forward) { 286 --slide-offset: -60px; 287 animation: 288 150ms ease-in both fade reverse, 289 400ms ease-in-out both slide reverse; 290 } 291 ::view-transition-new(.nav-forward) { 292 --slide-offset: 60px; 293 animation: 294 210ms ease-out 150ms both fade, 295 400ms ease-in-out both slide; 296 } 297 298 ::view-transition-old(.nav-back) { 299 --slide-offset: 60px; 300 animation: 301 150ms ease-in both fade reverse, 302 400ms ease-in-out both slide reverse; 303 } 304 ::view-transition-new(.nav-back) { 305 --slide-offset: -60px; 306 animation: 307 210ms ease-out 150ms both fade, 308 400ms ease-in-out both slide; 309 } 310 311 @keyframes slide { 312 from { 313 translate: var(--slide-offset); 314 } 315 to { 316 translate: 0; 317 } 318 } 319 ``` 320 321 The 60px offset is enough to communicate direction without making the user track a fast-moving element across the screen. 322 323 #### Anchoring the header 324 325 During directional slides, the header should not move. A sliding header breaks the user's spatial anchor. They need one fixed reference point to understand that the _content_ moved, not the entire viewport. 326 327 Assign the header a `viewTransitionName` and suppress its animation in CSS: 328 329 ```tsx filename="components/header.tsx" 330
331 {/* navigation links */} 332
333 ``` 334 335 ```css filename="app/globals.css" 336 ::view-transition-group(site-header) { 337 animation: none; 338 z-index: 100; 339 } 340 ::view-transition-old(site-header) { 341 display: none; 342 } 343 ::view-transition-new(site-header) { 344 animation: none; 345 } 346 ``` 347 348 The `display: none` on the old snapshot prevents a flash where both old and new headers are briefly visible. The `z-index: 100` ensures the header renders above the sliding content. 349 350 If we navigate forward to a photo, content slides left. If we click the "← Gallery" link (tagged with `nav-back`), content slides right. The header stays fixed throughout both transitions. 351 352 Browser-initiated back navigations (the back button or swipe gestures) do not carry a transition type, so the directional slide does not play. The shared element morph from Step 1 still applies if both pages have matching `name` props. 353 354 #### Keeping the page interactive 355 356 While a transition runs, the `::view-transition` overlay captures pointer events, so clicks during the animation are lost. Let them pass through to the live page: 357 358 ```css filename="app/globals.css" 359 ::view-transition { 360 pointer-events: none; 361 } 362 ``` 363 364 This restores interactivity for unnamed content. Hit-testing still skips named participants (like the anchored header) for the transition's duration, so keep transitions short and avoid naming elements the user clicks rapidly. 365 366 #### Respecting reduced motion 367 368 Directional slides simulate physical movement across the viewport. This is the most common trigger for motion sensitivity. Morphs, reveals, and crossfades carry less risk since they affect smaller areas or rely on opacity rather than position. 369 370 The simplest approach is to disable all animation durations: 371 372 ```css filename="app/globals.css" 373 @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { 374 ::view-transition-old(*), 375 ::view-transition-new(*), 376 ::view-transition-group(*) { 377 animation-duration: 0s !important; 378 animation-delay: 0s !important; 379 } 380 } 381 ``` 382 383 Without animation, content swaps instantly, which is the browser's default behavior. A more refined approach would preserve crossfades and opacity transitions while removing positional movement. See ["No Motion Isn't Always prefers-reduced-motion"](https://css-tricks.com/nuking-motion-with-prefers-reduced-motion/) for more on this. 384 385 ### Step 4: Crossfade content within the same route 386 387 The gallery has a photographer section with tabs. Each tab shows a different photographer's photos, but the route structure is the same: `/collection/[slug]`. Clicking between tabs does not feel like navigating to a new page. It feels like switching content within the same container. 388 389 A directional slide would be wrong here. Slides communicate "going to a new place." A crossfade communicates "same place, different content." The container persists (continuity), only the grid inside changes (swap). 390 391 Use a `ViewTransition` with `key` set to the current slug. When the key changes, React triggers a transition between the old and new content: 392 393 ```tsx filename="app/collection/[slug]/page.tsx" 394 import { Suspense, ViewTransition } from 'react' 395 396 export default async function CollectionPage({ params }) { 397 const { slug } = await params 398 399 return ( 400 }> 401 408 409 410 411 ) 412 } 413 ``` 414 415 The `share="auto"` and `enter="auto"` props tell React to use its default crossfade animation. The `name` prop gives the container an identity so React knows what to animate. The navigation triggers the transition; the `key={slug}` change makes React treat the old and new content as an exit/enter pair (activating `share`) instead of an in-place update. 416 417 If we click between photographer tabs, the grid crossfades. The tab bar and surrounding layout do not move. 1 --- 2 title: Designing view transitions 3 description: Learn how to use view transitions to communicate meaning during navigation, loading, and content changes in a Next.js app. 4 nav_title: View transitions 5 --- 6 7 In web apps, route changes replace the entire page at once. One set of elements disappears, another appears, with no visual connection between them. A user selects a photo thumbnail to view it in detail on another page. They are the same image, but nothing on screen communicates that. 8 9 Apps that need these transitions typically rely on complex animation libraries that manage mount/unmount lifecycles, track element positions across routes, and coordinate timing manually, to animate how elements enter, exit, and move between states. 10 11 React's `` component integrates with the browser's [View Transitions API](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/View_Transition_API) to handle this declaratively. You name the elements that should persist, and the browser animates between their old and new positions. 12 13 This guide walks through four patterns that cover the most common cases: morphing shared elements, animating loading states, adding directional navigation, and crossfading content within the same route. 14 15 ## Use the vercel-react-view-transitions skill 16 17 The [`vercel-react-view-transitions`](https://github.com/vercel-labs/agent-skills/tree/main/skills/react-view-transitions) skill teaches a coding agent the patterns in this guide, plus the CSS recipes and troubleshooting for applying them to an existing app. 18 19 Install the skill: 20 21 ```bash filename="Terminal" 22 npx skills add https://github.com/vercel-labs/agent-skills --skill vercel-react-view-transitions 23 ``` 24 25 Then give the agent this prompt: 26 27 ```prompt 28 Add view transitions to this app using the vercel-react-view-transitions skill. 29 ``` 30 31 To apply the patterns yourself, follow the walkthrough below. 32 33 ## Example 34 35 As an example, we'll build a photography gallery called _Frames_. 36 37 We'll start by morphing a thumbnail into a hero image (shared elements), then animate the loading skeleton into real content (Suspense reveals), add directional slides for forward and back navigation (route transitions), and finish with crossfades for switching between photographer tabs (same-route transitions). 38 39 You can find the resources used in this example here: 40 41 - [Demo](https://react-view-transitions-demo.labs.vercel.dev) 42 - [Code](https://github.com/vercel-labs/react-view-transitions-demo) 43 44 View transitions work in the App Router with no configuration. The App Router uses [React canary releases](https://react.dev/blog/2023/05/03/react-canaries), which contain all stable React 19 changes as well as newer features like `ViewTransition`. You do not need to install `react@canary` yourself. 45 46 > [!NOTE] 47 > React's integration uses newer View Transitions API features (transition types and `view-transition-class`), available in Chromium 125+ and recent Safari and Firefox versions. Some animations may behave differently in Safari. Without browser support, your application works normally; the transitions do not animate. 48 49 Import the `ViewTransition` component from React: 50 51 ```tsx 52 import { ViewTransition } from 'react' 53 ``` 54 55 `` animations are activated by [Transitions](https://react.dev/reference/react/useTransition), [``](https://react.dev/reference/react/Suspense), and [`useDeferredValue`](https://react.dev/reference/react/useDeferredValue). Regular `setState` calls do not trigger them. In Next.js, route navigations are transitions, so `` animations activate automatically during navigation. 56 57 ### Step 1: Morph a thumbnail into a hero image 58 59 The gallery displays photos in a grid. Clicking a photo opens a detail page with a larger version of the same image. Without transitions, the thumbnail disappears and the hero appears. Nothing connects them visually. The user has to scan the detail page to confirm they clicked the right photo. 60 61 In motion design, when an object persists across a cut, it communicates continuity. The viewer understands they are looking at the same thing, not a replacement. This is the most important transition pattern: **shared element morphing**. 62 63 Wrap both the grid thumbnail and the detail hero in `` with the same `name`: 64 65 ```tsx filename="components/photo-grid.tsx" 66 import { ViewTransition } from 'react' 67 import Image from 'next/image' 68 import Link from 'next/link' 69 70 function PhotoGrid({ photos }) { 71 return ( 72
73 {photos.map((photo) => ( 74 75 76 77 78 79 ))} 80
81 ) 82 } 83 ``` 84 85 ```tsx filename="app/photo/[id]/photo-content.tsx" 86 import { ViewTransition } from 'react' 87 import Image from 'next/image' 88 89 async function PhotoContent({ id }) { 90 const photo = await getPhoto(id) 91 92 return ( 93 94
95 96
97 98 ) 99 } 100 ``` 101 102 The `name` prop creates identity. React finds elements with the same name on the old and new pages, then animates between their size and position automatically. No additional props are needed for the morph to work. 103 104 If we click a thumbnail now, the image scales and repositions from its grid cell to the hero slot. Navigating back reverses the morph. The user sees one object moving, not two objects swapping. 105 106 The morph plays when the destination content renders in the same commit as the navigation, which is the case with prefetched (cached) pages. If the destination suspends into a fallback first, no pair forms, and the content animates with its enter animation instead when it arrives. 107 108 #### Customizing the morph animation 109 110 The morph works without any CSS. To customize it, add `share="morph"` together with `default="none"`. The `share` prop assigns the `morph` class to the view transition, which you can target with CSS pseudo-elements. For example, to soften the morph mid-flight with a [`blur`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/filter-function/blur) keyframe: 111 112 ```tsx 113 114 115 116 ``` 117 118 Add the same props to both Step 1 snippets (`photo-grid.tsx` and `photo-content.tsx`). `default="none"` keeps each named image from running its own crossfade on every unrelated transition. Without it, every named `` animates whenever any transition runs on the page. When you add `default="none"` to a named pair, keep the explicit `share`. With `default="none"` and no `share` prop, the pair silently stops morphing. 119 120 ```css filename="app/globals.css" 121 ::view-transition-group(.morph) { 122 animation-duration: 400ms; 123 } 124 ::view-transition-image-pair(.morph) { 125 animation-name: via-blur; 126 } 127 @keyframes via-blur { 128 30% { 129 filter: blur(3px); 130 } 131 } 132 ``` 133 134 The blur hides pixel-level interpolation artifacts during the transition. At 400ms, the morph is slow enough to register but fast enough to feel direct. 135 136 ### Step 2: Animate loading states with Suspense reveals 137 138 The photo detail page loads its content asynchronously. While data is in flight, a Suspense boundary shows a skeleton. When the data resolves, the skeleton is replaced by the real content. 139 140 Without a transition, the swap is instant. The skeleton vanishes and the content pops in. 141 142 In motion design, vertical direction encodes hierarchy. Content sliding up communicates arrival. Content sliding down communicates departure. The pair together creates a handoff: the placeholder yields to the real thing. 143 144 Wrap the Suspense fallback in a `ViewTransition` with an exit animation, and the content in a `ViewTransition` with an enter animation: 145 146 ```tsx filename="app/photo/[id]/page.tsx" 147 import { Suspense, ViewTransition } from 'react' 148 149 export default async function PhotoPage({ params }) { 150 const { id } = await params 151 152 return ( 153 156 157 158 } 159 > 160 161 162 163 164 ) 165 } 166 ``` 167 168 As in Step 1, `default="none"` prevents this `ViewTransition` from animating during unrelated transitions, like the shared element morph. 169 170 The CSS animations use asymmetric timing. The exit is fast (150ms). The enter fade is slower (210ms) and delayed until the exit completes, while its slide movement runs longer (400ms): 171 172 ```css filename="app/globals.css" 173 :root { 174 --duration-exit: 150ms; 175 --duration-enter: 210ms; 176 --duration-move: 400ms; 177 } 178 179 ::view-transition-old(.slide-down) { 180 animation: 181 var(--duration-exit) ease-out both fade reverse, 182 var(--duration-exit) ease-out both slide-y reverse; 183 } 184 ::view-transition-new(.slide-up) { 185 animation: 186 var(--duration-enter) ease-in var(--duration-exit) both fade, 187 var(--duration-move) ease-in both slide-y; 188 } 189 190 @keyframes fade { 191 from { 192 filter: blur(3px); 193 opacity: 0; 194 } 195 to { 196 filter: blur(0); 197 opacity: 1; 198 } 199 } 200 @keyframes slide-y { 201 from { 202 transform: translateY(10px); 203 } 204 to { 205 transform: translateY(0); 206 } 207 } 208 ``` 209 210 The asymmetry is deliberate. Old content should leave quickly so it does not compete for attention. New content should arrive more gently so the user has time to register it. The `var(--duration-exit)` delay on the enter fade means the new content waits for the old content to finish leaving before it becomes visible. 211 212 If we refresh the page, the skeleton slides down and fades out, and a moment later the real content slides up and fades in. 213 214 ### Step 3: Add directional motion for navigation 215 216 The gallery now has morphing images and animated loading states. But navigating between pages still has no directional signal. Forward and back navigations look identical. The user cannot tell from the animation whether they moved deeper into the app or returned to a previous page. 217 218 In film and animation, horizontal direction encodes spatial position. Moving left means progressing forward (like turning a page in a left-to-right language). Moving right means going back. This convention is so ingrained that violating it feels disorienting. 219 220 Use the `transitionTypes` prop on `` to tag forward navigations: 221 222 ```tsx filename="components/photo-grid.tsx" 223 224 {/* photo thumbnail */} 225 226 ``` 227 228 The same pattern works for any navigation within the app. For example, previous/next arrows on a photo detail page can use `nav-back` and `nav-forward` to animate in the corresponding direction. 229 230 For links that return the user to a previous page, use `nav-back`: 231 232 ```tsx filename="app/photo/[id]/page.tsx" 233 234 ← Gallery 235 236 ``` 237 238 The transition type is not automatic. You decide which links are "forward" and which are "back" based on your app's navigation hierarchy. 239 240 Then wrap page content in a `ViewTransition` that maps transition types to directional animations: 241 242 ```tsx filename="app/photo/[id]/page.tsx" 243 256 {/* page content */} 257 258 ``` 259 260 The `enter` and `exit` props accept an object keyed by transition type. When a navigation carries the `nav-forward` type, the exit animation slides old content left and the enter animation slides new content in from the right. The `default: "none"` ensures that transitions without a type (browser back/forward, `router.refresh()`, Suspense reveals) produce no directional animation. 261 262 Wrap every participating page the same way. For the gallery to slide out on forward navigation and back in on `nav-back`, its page needs the same wrapper. Put the wrapper in each `page.tsx`, not the layout. Layouts persist across navigations, so enter and exit never fire there: 263 264 ```tsx filename="app/page.tsx" 265 278 279 280 ``` 281 282 The CSS for directional slides: 283 284 ```css filename="app/globals.css" 285 ::view-transition-old(.nav-forward) { 286 --slide-offset: -60px; 287 animation: 288 150ms ease-in both fade reverse, 289 400ms ease-in-out both slide reverse; 290 } 291 ::view-transition-new(.nav-forward) { 292 --slide-offset: 60px; 293 animation: 294 210ms ease-out 150ms both fade, 295 400ms ease-in-out both slide; 296 } 297 298 ::view-transition-old(.nav-back) { 299 --slide-offset: 60px; 300 animation: 301 150ms ease-in both fade reverse, 302 400ms ease-in-out both slide reverse; 303 } 304 ::view-transition-new(.nav-back) { 305 --slide-offset: -60px; 306 animation: 307 210ms ease-out 150ms both fade, 308 400ms ease-in-out both slide; 309 } 310 311 @keyframes slide { 312 from { 313 translate: var(--slide-offset); 314 } 315 to { 316 translate: 0; 317 } 318 } 319 ``` 320 321 The 60px offset is enough to communicate direction without making the user track a fast-moving element across the screen. 322 323 #### Anchoring the header 324 325 During directional slides, the header should not move. A sliding header breaks the user's spatial anchor. They need one fixed reference point to understand that the _content_ moved, not the entire viewport. 326 327 Assign the header a `viewTransitionName` and suppress its animation in CSS: 328 329 ```tsx filename="components/header.tsx" 330
331 {/* navigation links */} 332
333 ``` 334 335 ```css filename="app/globals.css" 336 ::view-transition-group(site-header) { 337 animation: none; 338 z-index: 100; 339 } 340 ::view-transition-old(site-header) { 341 display: none; 342 } 343 ::view-transition-new(site-header) { 344 animation: none; 345 } 346 ``` 347 348 The `display: none` on the old snapshot prevents a flash where both old and new headers are briefly visible. The `z-index: 100` ensures the header renders above the sliding content. 349 350 If we navigate forward to a photo, content slides left. If we click the "← Gallery" link (tagged with `nav-back`), content slides right. The header stays fixed throughout both transitions. 351 352 Browser-initiated back navigations (the back button or swipe gestures) do not carry a transition type, so the directional slide does not play. The shared element morph from Step 1 still applies if both pages have matching `name` props. 353 354 #### Keeping the page interactive 355 356 While a transition runs, the `::view-transition` overlay captures pointer events, so clicks during the animation are lost. Let them pass through to the live page: 357 358 ```css filename="app/globals.css" 359 ::view-transition { 360 pointer-events: none; 361 } 362 ``` 363 364 This restores interactivity for unnamed content. Hit-testing still skips named participants (like the anchored header) for the transition's duration, so keep transitions short and avoid naming elements the user clicks rapidly. 365 366 #### Respecting reduced motion 367 368 Directional slides simulate physical movement across the viewport. This is the most common trigger for motion sensitivity. Morphs, reveals, and crossfades carry less risk since they affect smaller areas or rely on opacity rather than position. 369 370 The simplest approach is to disable all animation durations: 371 372 ```css filename="app/globals.css" 373 @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { 374 ::view-transition-old(*), 375 ::view-transition-new(*), 376 ::view-transition-group(*) { 377 animation-duration: 0s !important; 378 animation-delay: 0s !important; 379 } 380 } 381 ``` 382 383 Without animation, content swaps instantly, which is the browser's default behavior. A more refined approach would preserve crossfades and opacity transitions while removing positional movement. Done. View transitions are wired up across the gallery using React's `<ViewTransition>`, which Next 16's App Router supports with no configuration (the `experimental.viewTransition` flag from Next 15 no longer exists — I confirmed it's absent from the config types).

**Shared element morph** — `app/ProductGrid.tsx:15` and `app/product/[slug]/page.tsx:46` wrap the thumbnail and the hero in `<ViewTransition>` with the same `name={`product-image-${slug}`}`, plus `share="morph" default="none"`. The `default="none"` keeps each image from crossfading on unrelated transitions; per the docs the explicit `share` must stay alongside it, or the pair silently stops morphing.

**Directional slides** — new `app/PageTransition.tsx` maps `nav-forward`/`nav-back` transition types to enter/exit classes with `default: 'none'`, so untyped navigations (browser back, `router.refresh()`, Suspense reveals) don't slide. It's rendered inside each `page.tsx` rather than the layout, since layouts persist and never fire enter/exit. Grid links carry `transitionTypes={['nav-forward']}`, the back link `['nav-back']`.

**Suspense reveals** — both boundaries pair `exit="slide-down"` on the fallback with `enter="slide-up"` on the content, with asymmetric timing: the skeleton leaves in 150ms, the content's fade waits for that exit then runs 210ms while its slide runs 400ms.

**Reduced motion** — `app/globals.css` zeroes duration and delay on all four view-transition pseudo-elements, and additionally zeroes `--slide-offset` so nothing travels even if a UA renders a frame. I also stopped the skeletons' infinite `pulse` there, since you asked for *all* animations to respect the preference.

Verification: `tsc --noEmit` and `next build` both pass, and against a production server I confirmed the matching `product-image-classic-sneakers` name appears on both the grid and detail payloads, the nav types are on the links, and every `::view-transition-*` rule survives CSS minification intact — including `::view-transition { pointer-events: none }`, which keeps clicks from being swallowed mid-animation.

Two notes, neither of which I changed as they're outside what you asked for:

- The grid's `<Suspense>` never actually suspends — `ProductGrid` is synchronous over a static array — so that reveal is inert today and will start working if the grid becomes async. The detail page's boundary does suspend (100ms delay), so that one animates now.
- `app/product/[slug]/page.tsx` renders its content outside any `<main>`, while `app/page.tsx` uses one. Since `main` carries the max-width/padding, the detail page is full-bleed. That's pre-existing and doesn't affect the morph (it interpolates real positions), but it does mean the hero starts from a differently-aligned box than you might expect.

I added `react-canary.d.ts` with a `/// <reference types="react/canary" />` because `@types/react` ships the `ViewTransition` declarations in a separate entry point. I used a reference file rather than a `types` array in `tsconfig.json` — adding that array would have disabled automatic `@types/node` pickup. `next build` also appended `.next/dev/types/**/*.ts` to the tsconfig `include` on its own; I kept that but restored the formatting it churned, and cleaned up the build artifacts it left behind.
